\chapter{Gustar — the Verb Built the Other Way Round}
\label{ch:spanish-gustar}
\hlchaptermodality{163}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build a gustar sentence the way Spanish builds it, with the thing liked as the subject.}

me gusta el libro is the book pleasing me, so the verb agrees with the book.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[gustar]{gustar — the verb that runs backwards}

\label{lesson:ES-C35-gustar}



\begin{quote}
Back in the introductions you learned \textbf{mucho gusto} — \textquotedblleft{}much pleasure\textquotedblright{}. Here is the verb that noun belongs to, assembled the opposite way round from English. It is the single thing in Spanish that trips English speakers up hardest.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{g-hard} — a hard \emph{g} before \emph{u}: \emph{goos-TAR}.
  \item \texttt{s-clear} — a clean hissing \emph{s}, never a \emph{z} buzz.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gustar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{gustāre}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to taste}\textquotedblright{}. English kept the root and stayed close to the tongue:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{gusto} — doing something with relish, that is, with a taste for it.
  \item \textbf{gustatory} — of the sense of taste.
  \item \textbf{disgust} — \emph{dis-} \textquotedblleft{}away\textquotedblright{} + taste: what you spit back out.
  \item \textbf{degustation}, a tasting menu; and through French, \textbf{ragout}.
\end{itemize}

Spanish's own \textbf{el gusto} — the \emph{gusto} of \emph{mucho gusto} — still holds both senses: taste on the tongue, and pleasure taken in a thing. The verb followed the second: \emph{gustar} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to please}\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the thing you like is the subject}]
English says \textbf{I} like the book: the liker is the subject. Spanish has no such sentence. It says \textbf{Me gusta el libro} — \textquotedblleft{}the book is pleasing \textbf{to me}\textquotedblright{}.

Everything follows from that:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el libro} is the \textbf{subject}, which is why the verb is \emph{gusta}, third person.
  \item \emph{me} is the person it happens \textbf{to}, not the one doing anything.
\end{itemize}

So the verb agrees with the \textbf{thing}, never with you:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you mean} & \textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{why} \\
\midrule
I like the book & \textbf{Me gusta el libro} & one book, so \emph{gusta} \\
I like books & \textbf{Me gustan los libros} & many books, so \emph{gustan} \\
I like reading & \textbf{Me gusta leer} & one action, so \emph{gusta} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

To change who is pleased, change the little word in front, not the verb: \textbf{me} (to me), \textbf{te} (to you), \textbf{le} (to him, her, \emph{usted}), \textbf{nos} (to us), \textbf{les} (to them).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Careful.} There is no \emph{yo gusto el libro}. \emph{Yo gusto} is a real sentence — it means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I} am pleasing\textquotedblright{} — just not the one you were reaching for.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Me gusta el café\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Me gustan los libros\textquotedblright{} — the verb follows the thing
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Te gusta tomar café\textquotedblright{} — you like drinking coffee
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Me gusta ayudar\textquotedblright{} — I like helping
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gustar\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}gusto, disgust, gustatory\textquotedblright{} — the tasting family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In \emph{me gusta el libro}, what is the subject? (\textbf{El libro}.) Why is it \emph{me gustan los libros}? (The verb agrees with \emph{los libros}, which is plural.) What did \emph{gustāre} mean, and name an English cousin. (\textbf{To taste}; \emph{gusto, disgust}.) And what would \emph{yo gusto} actually mean? (\textbf{I} am pleasing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
